text: The orchestration layer runs the happy path correctly. This lesson adds the two things every real deployment needs before it can be trusted unattended: proper failure handling, and a live, trustworthy cost ledger.

We'll apply the retry and fallback decision table from Chapter 3 inside this project's actual loop, build a cost ledger that updates per iteration, set a real circuit-breaker ceiling, and test all of it with injected synthetic failures rather than waiting for a real one.

Here's the ledger, concretely. Every submission appends an entry: iteration, attempt, device, shots, cost, status, latency. A normal submission costs twelve dollars. If iteration twenty-three fails once before succeeding on retry, the ledger shows two twelve-dollar entries — one failed, one done — never silently collapsed into a single successful-looking line.
And here's exactly where those fields come from in practice — a real Amazon Braket task detail page: status, shots, cost, all visible for one real submission, the same shape every ledger entry needs.

The circuit breaker checks cumulative ledger cost against a ceiling with headroom built in — twelve hundred dollars, twenty-five percent over the planned nine hundred sixty. Here's the real control that ceiling is built on: Amazon Braket's own per-QPU spending limits. If cumulative cost crosses that line before iteration eighty completes, the loop halts immediately and raises an alert.

Testing this doesn't wait for a real device to fail at the right moment. A fault-injection layer wraps the backend adapter and forces exactly these job states on command — the same states in this real provider diagram — letting you verify deterministically that a device-offline failure triggers backoff, a validation failure doesn't retry, and four consecutive failures correctly triggers the fallback path.
Next lesson is the final architecture review — checking this finished system against the course's own five-mistake checklist, not just confirming that it runs.
